title: Placebo and Nocebo Effects: The Advantage of Measuring Expectations and Psychological Factors
research_objective: Investigate the interplay between psychological factors, expectations of low and high pain, and placebo and nocebo effects.
methodology: Used a well-validated conditioning paradigm with contact heat thermal stimuli. Visual cues alerted participants about pain levels.
intervention: High, medium, and low levels of pain associated with red, yellow, and green cues, respectively.
control_group: No specific control group mentioned, only placebo and nocebo manipulations.
main_findings: Robust placebo hypolagesic and nocebo hyperalgesic responses correlated with expectancy of low and high pain. Psychological factors per se did not influence expectations.
limitations: No explicit limitations mentioned in the excerpt.
conclusions: Psychological factors and expectation measures may offer advantages in predicting placebo and nocebo effects related to experimental acute pain.

title: Application of Bayes’ Theorem in Valuating Depression Tests
authors: Marco Tommasi; Grazia Ferrara; Aristide Saggino
research_objective: To evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of depression tests using Bayes' theorem.
methodology: Analysis of published works reporting sensitivity and specificity of depression tests.
main_findings: None of the tested depression tests can reach a satisfactory level of diagnostic accuracy, possibly due to the lack of an optimal procedure to select test items and subjects with clearly defined pathological symptoms.
limitations: No explicit limitations are mentioned in the provided excerpt.
conclusions: The application of Bayes' theorem is a valid alternative to make diagnoses on the basis of the scores from psychological tests.

title: Putting the ‘Art’ Into the ‘Art of Medicine’: The Under-Explored Role of Artifacts in Placebo Studies
authors: Michael H. Bernstein; Cosima Locher; Tobias Kube; Sarah Buergler; Sif Stewart-Ferrer; Charlotte Blease
research_objective: To explore the role of artifacts in placebo studies and their potential impact on health outcomes.
main_findings: Non-medical artifacts, such as clinician clothing and office decor, can influence healthcare outcomes. Formal attire, especially white coats, is associated with positive patient perceptions and treatment preferences.
conclusions: A careful consideration of artifacts may carry significant potential in informing how placebo effects can be maximized, and nocebo effects minimized in clinical settings.

title: Placebo Effects on Stress, but Not on Pain Reports. A Multi-Experiment Study
authors: Sara Magelssen Vambheim; Hojjat Daniali; Magne Arve Flaten
research_objective: To investigate if (i) participant sex and (ii) experimenter sex influence placebo analgesia and subjective and physiological stress in two experiments employing a within-subject and a mixed design, respectively.
methodology: Participants received painful stimulations and a placebo cream. In Experiment One (N = 59), participants underwent a placebo condition (PC) and a natural history condition (NHC) in random order. A placebo cream was applied in the PC and then the heat stimulation temperature was surreptitiously lowered. Identical stimulations were administered in the NHC, but with no cream, no information, and no lowered temperature. In Experiment Two, participants (N = 93) were randomly assigned to three groups receiving either a placebo cream with lowered intensity of electric stimuli (Placebo, PG), a placebo cream (Cream-Control, CCG) without changing the stimuli, or lowered intensity but no cream (Pain-Control, PCG). All participants received the same stimuli in the post-test as in the pre-test. Four experimenters (two females) in Experiment One, and five experimenters (two females) in Experiment Two conducted the studies.
intervention: Placebo cream with lowered intensity of electric stimuli (PG), placebo cream (CCG) without changing the stimuli, or lowered intensity but no cream (PCG)
control_group: Natural History Condition (NHC) in Experiment One and Cream-Control (CCG) in Experiment Two
main_findings: No placebo effect was seen on pain. However, there were placebo effects on stress, moderated by participant and experimenter sex: in Experiment One, males in the PC had lower diastolic blood pressure (DBP) compared to males in the NHC. In Experiment Two, participants expected more cream effectiveness when a female experimenter administered it, and reported lower stress in the PG compared to the PCG when tested by females.
limitations: Low statistical power, within-subjects design, low sample size, only one experimenter from each sex, measuring BP only one time in each measurement point.
conclusions: Our findings highlight a distinction between placebo effects on pain and on associated stress. Second, female experimenters recorded lower physiological and subjective stress, higher effectiveness expectations, and lower pain from both sexes compared to male experimenters. Possible reasons for the failure to find a pain placebo effect are discussed.

title: Placebo stimulates neuroplasticity in depression: implications for clinical practice and research
intervention: Various treatments including electroconvulsive therapy, psychological therapy, exercise, and medication.
main_findings: Neuroplasticity in fronto-limbic areas is the unifying factor in placebo response and placebo effect.
limitations: The study by Ashar et al. (21) is an important advance in the understanding of placebo from a psychological perspective, but it fails to explain why placebos persist and do not naturally extinguish
conclusions: If placebo stimulates neuroplasticity in fronto-limbic areas in conditions other than depression, it can lead to a partially active treatment in other areas of medicine.

title: Cognitive distortion based explainable depression detection and analysis technologies for the adolescent internet users
authors: Bichen Wang; Yanyan Zhao; Xin Lu; Bing Qin
research_objective: Propose a new task, explainable depression detection, to not only automatically detect depression but also try to give clues to depression based on cognitive distortion theory.
methodology: Construct a multi-task learning model based on a pre-trained model to detect depression and identify cognitive distortion. Use word clouds for data analysis.
intervention: Semi-supervised learning and fine-tuning a pre-trained BERT model
main_findings: Our experimental results outperform the baseline results and interesting conclusions about adolescent depression are drawn. The model can detect post-level cognitive distortion information and user-level depression.
limitations: The dataset is still too small for deep learning techniques, and the distribution of data from social media may differ from the actual situation.
conclusions: Provide psychologists with effective clues about depression according to psychological theory, which can not only increase the credibility of the model but also help further correct this distorted information.
